q: In a eukaryotic cell, glycolysis takes place in the:
x: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm (cytosol) and needs no organelle. The later aerobic stages, the link reaction, Krebs cycle and electron transport chain, take place in mitochondria.

q: The correct order of the stages of aerobic respiration of glucose is:
o: Krebs cycle → glycolysis → link reaction → electron transport chain
Glycolysis → Krebs cycle → link reaction → electron transport chain
Link reaction → glycolysis → Krebs cycle → electron transport chain
Glycolysis → link reaction → Krebs cycle → electron transport chain
x: Glucose is split into pyruvate in glycolysis. Pyruvate becomes acetyl CoA in the link reaction, acetyl CoA is oxidized in the Krebs cycle, and the reduced coenzymes pass their electrons to the electron transport chain.

q: How many ATP molecules are used up in the first (energy-investment) steps of glycolysis for each glucose molecule?
x: Two ATP are spent to phosphorylate glucose and then fructose-6-phosphate. Later steps make four ATP, so glycolysis gives a net gain of two ATP.

q: The first reaction of glycolysis is:
o: Splitting of glucose into two pyruvate molecules
Removal of carbon dioxide from glucose
Phosphorylation of glucose to glucose-6-phosphate using ATP
x: Glycolysis begins by adding a phosphate from ATP to glucose, forming glucose-6-phosphate. This activates the sugar and keeps it inside the cell. No carbon dioxide is released in glycolysis.

q: In glycolysis, fructose-1,6-bisphosphate is split into:
o: One four-carbon and one two-carbon molecule
x: The six-carbon fructose-1,6-bisphosphate splits into two three-carbon sugar phosphates (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, also called PGAL). Each is then oxidized to pyruvate. Acetyl CoA forms later, in the link reaction.

q: Substrate-level phosphorylation means that ATP is made by:
o: The flow of protons through ATP synthase
Direct transfer of a phosphate group from a substrate molecule to ADP
x: In substrate-level phosphorylation an enzyme moves a phosphate from a high-energy substrate straight onto ADP, as happens in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle. ATP made by proton flow through ATP synthase is oxidative phosphorylation.

q: The products of glycolysis from one molecule of glucose are:
o: One pyruvate, one NADH and a net gain of one ATP
Two acetyl CoA, two carbon dioxide and two NADH
Two pyruvate, two FADH2 and a net gain of four ATP
Two pyruvate, two NADH and a net gain of two ATP
x: Each glucose gives two pyruvate, two NADH and a net gain of two ATP (four made, two used). FADH2 is not made in glycolysis, and acetyl CoA and carbon dioxide come from the link reaction.

q: Which statement about glycolysis is correct?
o: It needs oxygen as the final electron acceptor
It does not need oxygen and occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration
It takes place only in animal cells
It releases most of the ATP made from glucose
x: Glycolysis needs no oxygen, so it is the common first stage of both aerobic and anaerobic respiration in almost all organisms. It gives only a small part of the total ATP; most comes from the electron transport chain.

q: In eukaryotic cells, pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA (the link reaction) in the:
x: Pyruvate made in the cytoplasm is carried into the mitochondrion, where it is converted to acetyl CoA in the matrix. The Krebs cycle also runs in the matrix.

q: During the link reaction, each pyruvate molecule:
o: Gains a carbon atom and becomes citrate
Is reduced to lactate by NADH
Is split into two molecules of glycerol
Loses carbon dioxide and is oxidized, forming acetyl CoA and NADH
x: Pyruvate (3C) undergoes oxidative decarboxylation: one carbon leaves as carbon dioxide, hydrogen is passed to NAD+, and the two-carbon acetyl group joins coenzyme A. Reduction to lactate happens only without oxygen.

q: For each molecule of glucose, the link reaction produces:
o: One carbon dioxide and one NADH
Two carbon dioxide and two NADH
Four carbon dioxide and two FADH2
Two carbon dioxide and two ATP
x: One glucose gives two pyruvate, and each pyruvate releases one carbon dioxide and forms one NADH in the link reaction. So the total per glucose is two of each. No ATP is made in this step.

q: The Krebs cycle is also known as the:
x: The Krebs cycle is called the citric acid cycle (or tricarboxylic acid cycle) after citrate, the first compound formed in it. The Calvin cycle is in photosynthesis, and the ornithine cycle makes urea.

q: The Krebs cycle begins when acetyl CoA (2C) combines with:
x: The two-carbon acetyl group joins four-carbon oxaloacetate to make six-carbon citrate. By the end of the cycle oxaloacetate is regenerated, ready to take the next acetyl group.

q: How many molecules of carbon dioxide are released in one turn of the Krebs cycle?
x: Each turn takes in a two-carbon acetyl group and releases two carbon dioxide, as citrate (6C) is cut down to oxaloacetate (4C). Four carbon dioxide come from one glucose because the cycle turns twice.

q: How many turns of the Krebs cycle are needed to oxidize the acetyl CoA formed from one glucose molecule?
x: One glucose gives two pyruvate and so two acetyl CoA. Each acetyl CoA enters one turn of the cycle, so the cycle turns twice per glucose.

q: The reduced coenzymes formed in one turn of the Krebs cycle are:
x: Each turn makes three NADH and one FADH2, plus one ATP (or GTP) and two carbon dioxide. These reduced coenzymes carry hydrogen to the electron transport chain.

q: The Krebs cycle uses no oxygen directly, yet it stops when oxygen runs out. This is because:
o: Oxygen is a substrate of citrate formation
Oxygen is needed to carry pyruvate into the cytoplasm
Without oxygen the electron transport chain stops and NAD+ and FAD are not regenerated
Without oxygen acetyl CoA is converted into glucose
x: Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. If it is absent, the chain backs up, NADH and FADH2 cannot be oxidized, and the Krebs cycle runs out of the NAD+ and FAD it needs.

q: Of the six carbon atoms in one glucose molecule, how many are released as carbon dioxide in the Krebs cycle itself (not counting the link reaction)?
x: Two carbons leave as carbon dioxide in the link reaction (one per pyruvate). The remaining four, carried as two acetyl groups, are released as four carbon dioxide over the two turns of the Krebs cycle.

q: In aerobic respiration of glucose, carbon dioxide is released during:
o: Glycolysis and the electron transport chain
The Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain
The link reaction and the Krebs cycle
x: Carbon dioxide is given off when pyruvate is decarboxylated in the link reaction and during the Krebs cycle. Glycolysis and the electron transport chain release no carbon dioxide.

q: The final acceptor of electrons in the electron transport chain of aerobic respiration is:
x: At the end of the chain, oxygen accepts electrons and combines with hydrogen ions to form water. This is why aerobic respiration needs oxygen.

q: The carriers of the electron transport chain are located in the:
x: The electron carriers and ATP synthase are built into the inner mitochondrial membrane. Its folds, the cristae, give a large surface area for many chains.

q: As electrons pass along the electron transport chain, the energy released is used to pump protons (H+):
o: From the matrix into the intermembrane space
From the intermembrane space into the matrix
From the cytoplasm into the nucleus
Out of the cell across the plasma membrane
x: Carrier proteins pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space. This builds up a high proton concentration between the two membranes, which is then used to make ATP.

q: According to the chemiosmotic theory, ATP synthase makes ATP using energy from:
o: Protons flowing back into the matrix down their concentration gradient
x: Protons pumped into the intermembrane space flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase. This flow drives the joining of ADP and phosphate into ATP, which is called oxidative phosphorylation.

q: Cytochromes, the electron carriers of the respiratory chain, contain which metal that is alternately oxidized and reduced?
x: Cytochromes contain a haem group with iron, which switches between Fe3+ and Fe2+ as it accepts and passes on electrons. Magnesium is the central metal of chlorophyll.

q: Cyanide blocks the last carrier of the electron transport chain (cytochrome oxidase). The immediate effect in a cell is that:
o: Glycolysis stops at once because glucose cannot enter the cell
Oxygen is converted into carbon dioxide
Electrons cannot pass to oxygen, so oxidative phosphorylation stops
Fatty acids are respired instead of glucose
x: With cytochrome oxidase blocked, electrons cannot reach oxygen, the chain stops and proton pumping ends. Most ATP production fails, which is why cyanide is so poisonous. Glycolysis can still continue for a while.

q: Compared with one FADH2, one NADH oxidized in the electron transport chain:
o: Yields less ATP, because NADH carries fewer electrons
Yields the same ATP, because both carry two electrons
Yields no ATP, because NADH is used only in glycolysis
Yields more ATP, because its electrons enter the chain at an earlier point
x: NADH passes its electrons to the first carrier, so they drive more proton pumps. FADH2 enters further along the chain and bypasses the first pump, so it yields less ATP.

q: In aerobic respiration of glucose, most of the ATP is produced by:
o: Substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs cycle
Oxidative phosphorylation linked to the electron transport chain
x: Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle make only a few ATP directly. Most ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation, powered by electrons from NADH and FADH2 passing along the electron transport chain.

q: The main role of NAD+ in respiration is to:
o: Accept hydrogen from substrates and carry it to the electron transport chain
Act as the final electron acceptor
Combine with acetyl groups to form citrate
Pump protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane
x: NAD+ is a coenzyme that picks up hydrogen (electrons) during glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle, becoming NADH. NADH then hands the electrons to the chain. Oxygen, not NAD+, is the final acceptor.

q: Allowing for the 2 ATP used at the start of glycolysis, the net number of ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation from one glucose in aerobic respiration is:
x: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but uses 2, a net of 2. The two turns of the Krebs cycle add 2 more (as ATP or GTP), giving a net of 4. Six is the total before subtracting the 2 ATP invested.

q: During hard exercise, when oxygen supply is short, human muscle cells convert pyruvate into:
x: Without enough oxygen, muscle cells reduce pyruvate to lactic acid (lactate). Ethanol and carbon dioxide are the products of alcoholic fermentation in yeast.

q: In the absence of oxygen, yeast cells convert glucose into:
x: Yeast carries out alcoholic fermentation: pyruvate loses carbon dioxide and is reduced to ethanol. This is used in baking and brewing. Carbon dioxide and water are the products of aerobic respiration.

q: The net yield of ATP from one glucose molecule by fermentation (anaerobic respiration) is:
x: In fermentation only glycolysis makes ATP, giving a net of two per glucose. The steps that form lactic acid or ethanol make no ATP.

q: In fermentation, pyruvate is converted into lactic acid or ethanol even though this makes no ATP. The purpose of this step is to:
o: Produce more carbon dioxide for the cell
Oxidize NADH back to NAD+ so that glycolysis can continue
x: Glycolysis needs a steady supply of NAD+. By using NADH to reduce pyruvate, the cell regenerates NAD+ and can keep making its two ATP per glucose without oxygen.

q: After hard exercise, a person keeps breathing deeply for some time. The extra oxygen is used mainly to:
o: Oxidize lactic acid or convert it back to glucose in the liver
Make more lactic acid in the muscles
x: Lactic acid built up during exercise is carried to the liver. There some is oxidized and the rest is converted back to pyruvate and glucose. The oxygen needed for this is called the oxygen debt.

q: Aerobic respiration releases far more ATP per glucose than anaerobic respiration because:
o: It produces lactic acid, which is rich in energy
It takes place only in the cytoplasm
Glucose is oxidized completely to carbon dioxide and water
x: In aerobic respiration glucose is fully oxidized, and most energy is captured through the electron transport chain. In anaerobic respiration much energy stays locked in lactic acid or ethanol.

q: The overall end products of aerobic respiration of glucose are:
x: The overall equation is glucose + 6 oxygen → 6 carbon dioxide + 6 water, with the energy captured as ATP. Lactic acid and ethanol are products of anaerobic respiration.

q: A cell's mitochondria are damaged so they cannot work. Which stage of respiration can the cell still carry out?
x: Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm, so it does not depend on mitochondria. The link reaction, Krebs cycle and electron transport chain all take place inside mitochondria.

q: Milk turns into curd (yoghurt) because certain bacteria carry out:
x: Lactic acid bacteria such as Lactobacillus ferment milk sugar into lactic acid, which sours and thickens the milk. Alcoholic fermentation, by yeast, produces ethanol instead.

q: In cells, glucose is oxidized in many small enzyme-controlled steps instead of all at once. The advantage is that:
o: Energy is released gradually and much of it is captured as ATP instead of being lost as heat
x: Burning glucose in one step would release its energy suddenly as heat. Releasing it in small steps lets the cell trap a large part of the energy in ATP.

q: ATP releases energy for cell work when it is:
o: Hydrolysed to ADP and inorganic phosphate
Combined with oxygen to form carbon dioxide
x: Breaking the bond to the terminal phosphate of ATP releases energy, forming ADP and inorganic phosphate. Respiration supplies the energy to rebuild ATP from ADP and phosphate.

q: Before proteins can be used as a respiratory fuel, they must first be:
o: Oxidized to carbon dioxide in the cytoplasm
x: Proteins are first broken down by protease enzymes into amino acids. Amino acids are then deaminated, and their carbon skeletons enter the respiratory pathways.

q: Deamination of an amino acid is the:
o: Removal of its carboxyl group as carbon dioxide
Joining of two amino acids by a peptide bond
Addition of phosphate to the amino acid
x: Deamination removes the amino (–NH2) group from an amino acid, leaving a carbon skeleton (a keto acid) that can be respired. The amino group becomes ammonia.

q: In humans, deamination of excess amino acids takes place mainly in the:
x: The liver deaminates excess amino acids and converts the toxic ammonia into urea. The kidneys only remove the urea from the blood; they do not make it.

q: The amino group removed during deamination is first released as ammonia, which in mammals is then converted into:
x: Ammonia is very toxic, so the liver combines it with carbon dioxide in the ornithine cycle to form urea. Urea is carried by the blood to the kidneys and excreted in urine.

q: After removal of its amino group, the amino acid alanine enters the respiratory pathway as:
x: Alanine is a three-carbon amino acid; without its amino group it becomes pyruvate. Pyruvate can then be converted to acetyl CoA and oxidized in the Krebs cycle.

q: The amino acid glutamate, after losing its amino group, enters the Krebs cycle directly as:
x: Glutamate is a five-carbon amino acid. Removing its amino group gives alpha-ketoglutarate, a five-carbon intermediate of the Krebs cycle. Different amino acids enter respiration at different points.

q: Which statement correctly describes how amino acids are respired?
o: All amino acids enter respiration only as glucose
Their carbon skeletons enter at different points, as pyruvate, acetyl CoA or Krebs cycle intermediates
Amino acids are respired with their amino groups still attached
Amino acids are respired only in anaerobic conditions
x: After deamination, the carbon skeletons of different amino acids are converted into pyruvate, acetyl CoA or various Krebs cycle intermediates. They then join the same pathway as glucose.

q: The body normally uses proteins as a major respiratory fuel only when:
o: A person has just eaten a meal rich in starch
Carbohydrate and fat reserves are nearly used up, as in starvation
The person is at rest after a normal meal
x: Proteins are mainly needed for growth, repair, enzymes and hormones. They become a major fuel only when carbohydrate and fat stores are exhausted, as in long starvation, when muscle protein is broken down.

q: A person changes to a diet very high in protein. Which change in the urine is expected?
o: Less urea, because proteins give no waste
More urea, from deamination of excess amino acids
x: Excess amino acids cannot be stored, so the liver deaminates them and turns the nitrogen into urea. More protein eaten means more urea to excrete.

q: Which molecule is the common entry point into the Krebs cycle for carbon from glucose, fatty acids and many amino acids?
x: Glucose (via pyruvate), fatty acids (via beta-oxidation) and many amino acids are all converted to acetyl CoA. It is the meeting point where the breakdown of carbohydrates, fats and proteins joins the Krebs cycle.

q: Before a fat (triglyceride) can be respired, the enzyme lipase hydrolyses it into:
x: Lipase breaks the ester bonds of a triglyceride, giving one glycerol and three fatty acids. Glycerol and fatty acids then enter respiration by different routes.

q: The glycerol part of a fat enters the respiratory pathway after being converted into:
o: Citrate, the first compound of the Krebs cycle
Many molecules of acetyl CoA by beta-oxidation
x: Glycerol is phosphorylated and converted into the three-carbon sugar phosphate PGAL, which goes through the rest of glycolysis to pyruvate. Beta-oxidation is the route for fatty acids, not glycerol.

q: Beta-oxidation breaks fatty acids down into:
x: Beta-oxidation cuts a fatty acid chain two carbons at a time, releasing each piece as acetyl CoA. The acetyl CoA then enters the Krebs cycle.

q: In human cells, beta-oxidation of fatty acids takes place mainly in the:
x: Fatty acids are carried into mitochondria and broken down in the matrix. The acetyl CoA produced there can enter the Krebs cycle directly, also in the matrix.

q: Each round of beta-oxidation of a fatty acid produces:
o: One pyruvate, one NADH and one ATP
Two acetyl CoA and two carbon dioxide
One acetyl CoA, one NADH and one FADH2
One glycerol, one NADH and one FADH2
x: Each round removes a two-carbon unit as acetyl CoA and passes hydrogen to one FAD and one NAD+, forming FADH2 and NADH. No carbon dioxide is released in beta-oxidation itself.

q: How many molecules of acetyl CoA are formed by complete beta-oxidation of one molecule of palmitic acid (16 carbons)?
x: Each acetyl CoA carries two carbons, so a 16-carbon chain gives 16 ÷ 2 = 8 acetyl CoA. Only seven rounds are needed, because the last round splits a four-carbon piece into two acetyl CoA.

q: Gram for gram, fats release more energy than carbohydrates when respired because fats:
o: Have more carbon–hydrogen bonds and relatively less oxygen
x: Fats are made mostly of long hydrocarbon chains, rich in hydrogen and poor in oxygen. They yield more hydrogen for the electron transport chain, and so more ATP per gram. Carbohydrates are already partly oxidized.

q: Compared with the same mass of carbohydrate, fat releases on respiration about:
x: Fat yields roughly 38–39 kJ per gram, against about 17 kJ per gram for carbohydrate and protein. That is a little more than twice as much, which is why fat is the body's main energy store.

q: Mature human red blood cells have no mitochondria. Which fuel and pathway can they use to make ATP?
o: Amino acids, by deamination and the Krebs cycle
Glycerol, by the electron transport chain
x: Beta-oxidation, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain all need mitochondria. Red blood cells can only break glucose down by glycolysis in the cytoplasm, forming lactate.

q: The breakdown of fatty acids is called beta-oxidation because:
o: It takes place only in beta cells of the pancreas
The bond cut lies at the beta (third) carbon, counting the carboxyl carbon as first
It is the second stage of respiration
x: In each round the beta carbon of the fatty acid is oxidized and the chain is cut there, releasing a two-carbon unit. The name has nothing to do with pancreatic beta cells or glucose.

q: In respiration, the function of coenzyme A is to:
o: Carry hydrogen to the electron transport chain
Pump protons into the intermembrane space
Break triglycerides into glycerol and fatty acids
Carry two-carbon acetyl groups into the Krebs cycle
x: Coenzyme A picks up acetyl groups from pyruvate, fatty acids and some amino acids, forming acetyl CoA. It hands the acetyl group to oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle. Hydrogen is carried by NAD and FAD.

q: The respiratory quotient (RQ) of a respiratory substrate is:
o: Volume of oxygen used ÷ volume of carbon dioxide released
Volume of carbon dioxide released ÷ volume of oxygen used
Number of ATP made ÷ number of glucose used
x: RQ = carbon dioxide produced ÷ oxygen consumed in the same time. Its value shows which substrate is being respired: about 1.0 for carbohydrate, about 0.7 for fat and about 0.8–0.9 for protein.

q: The RQ of fat (about 0.7) is lower than that of glucose (1.0). The reason is that fat:
o: Releases more carbon dioxide than the oxygen it uses
Contains little oxygen, so more oxygen is needed for each carbon dioxide formed
Contains nitrogen that uses up oxygen
x: Glucose has enough oxygen in its own molecule that it uses one oxygen for each carbon dioxide released, so RQ = 1. Fat is poor in oxygen, so extra oxygen is needed to oxidize its hydrogen to water, and RQ falls below 1.

q: Which statement correctly compares the respiration of glucose and fatty acids?
o: Fatty acids pass through glycolysis before the Krebs cycle
Glucose is converted into acetyl CoA by beta-oxidation
Glucose passes through glycolysis, while fatty acids are cut into acetyl CoA by beta-oxidation and skip glycolysis
Fatty acids are respired without using the Krebs cycle
x: Glucose goes through glycolysis and the link reaction to give acetyl CoA. Fatty acids reach acetyl CoA directly by beta-oxidation. From acetyl CoA onwards, both use the same Krebs cycle and electron transport chain.

q: Which of the following is NOT produced during beta-oxidation of a fatty acid?
x: Beta-oxidation produces acetyl CoA, NADH and FADH2 but releases no carbon dioxide. The carbon of fatty acids is released as carbon dioxide later, when acetyl CoA is oxidized in the Krebs cycle.
